Cytotoxic chemotherapy treats the underlying cancer but does not address the acute mechanical instability of the weakened femur.
Observation is contraindicated when there is high risk for a pathological fracture that would cause significant morbidity.
Cortical involvement >50% in a weight-bearing bone indicates a high risk of pathological fracture, requiring surgical stabilization.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 144 (Book Page): Surgical intervention may be warranted where there is ... an impending fracture (e.g. a large lytic lesion on a weight-bearing bone with more than 50% cortical involvement).

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A patient with advanced non-small cell lung cancer is started on the targeted therapy agent Erlotinib. During a follow-up visit, the patient complains of a new, itchy skin eruption on the face and upper chest. Based on the mechanism of the drug, which dermatological finding is most expected?
options: Vesicular lesions in a dermatomal distribution
Symmetrical purple-colored macules on the shins
Palmar-plantar redness and significant skin peeling
Acneiform rash involving the sebaceous areas
Painless telangiectasia in the previous radiation field
correctOption: Acneiform rash involving the sebaceous areas
optionExplanations: Dermatomal vesicles are characteristic of shingles (herpes zoster), not a specific side effect of EGFR inhibitors.
Symmetrical macules (like erythema nodosum) are not typically associated with EGFR inhibitor therapy.
Palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (hand-foot syndrome) is common with 5-FU, Capecitabine, and VEGF inhibitors, not EGFR inhibitors.
Acneiform rashes are a classic, mechanism-based side effect of Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) inhibitors like Erlotinib.
Telangiectasia is a late side effect of radiotherapy, occurring weeks or months after local radiation exposure.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): Acneiform rashes – EGFR inhibitors. (Table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment)

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: In the ongoing monitoring of a patient with advanced renal cell carcinoma receiving systemic therapy, the clinician uses the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST) to assess the effectiveness of the treatment. Which finding satisfies the criteria for a 'Partial Response' (PR)?
options: The total disappearance of all identified target lesions
The appearance of one new lesion despite tumor shrinkage
At least a 20% increase in the sum of the longest diameters
A decrease in size that does not reach the 30% threshold
At least a 30% decrease in the sum of the longest diameters
correctOption: At least a 30% decrease in the sum of the longest diameters
optionExplanations: Disappearance of all lesions is the definition of a Complete Response (CR), not a Partial Response.
The appearance of any new lesion automatically classifies the case as 'Progressive Disease' (PD).
A 20% increase in the sum of diameters is the definition for 'Progressive Disease' (PD).
Shrinkage that does not meet the 30% threshold is categorized as 'Stable Disease' (SD).
RECIST defines a Partial Response as at least a 30% reduction in the sum of the longest diameters of the target lesions.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 148 (Book Page): Partial response (PR) At least a 30% decrease in the sum of the longest diameter (LD) of target lesions, taking as reference the baseline sum LD.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A 58-year-old male with a history of Duke’s B colorectal cancer treated three years ago presents with a single 2 cm lesion in the right lobe of the liver. All other imaging is negative for metastatic disease. What is the expected five-year survival rate if this patient undergoes a successful surgical resection of this solitary metastasis?
options: Less than 5% due to the systemic nature of cancer
Fixed at 10% regardless of the type of intervention
Near 98% as the lesion is small and isolated
optionExplanations: Resection of solitary colorectal liver metastases significantly improves the 5-year survival rate to roughly 30-40%.
While metastatic cancer is generally poor, liver-only colorectal metastasis is a special case where surgery offers significant survival gains.
The survival is not fixed; the drastic improvement from 3% to 30-40% shows the impact of surgical intervention.
A 75% survival rate is too optimistic for metastatic disease; this rate is closer to Stage III disease outcomes.
A 98% survival rate is associated with Stage I breast cancer, not metastatic colorectal cancer.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 144 (Book Page): In colorectal cancer, successful resection of metastases improves 5-year survival from 3% to 30%–40%.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Emergency management of malignant spinal cord compression
statement: A 72-year-old man with known metastatic prostate cancer presents to the emergency department with a 48-hour history of severe, 'band-like' thoracic back pain that is worsened by coughing and lying flat. On examination, he has increased knee reflexes, extensor plantar responses, and a sensory level at T10. He is unable to void urine independently. After confirming the diagnosis with an urgent MRI, what is the most appropriate next pharmacological step according to standard protocols?
options: Administering Dexamethasone 16 mg intravenously or orally
Starting broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected sepsis
Applying a rigid spinal brace and complete bed rest alone
Commencing urgent cytotoxic chemotherapy with Docetaxel
correctOption: Administering Dexamethasone 16 mg intravenously or orally
optionExplanations: High-dose dexamethasone is the first-line treatment to reduce edema around the spinal cord and preserve neurological function.
The patient's symptoms are neurological and mechanical, not indicative of an infectious process requiring antibiotics.
Bisphosphonates are used for bone pain and hypercalcemia but do not reduce the neural edema causing cord compression.
Mechanical stabilization is important, but pharmacological intervention with steroids is the critical emergency step.
Chemotherapy may be used eventually, but it is too slow to address the acute emergency of cord compression.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 141 (Book Page): Management of suspected spinal cord compression ... Administer high-dose glucocorticoids: Dexamethasone 16 mg IV or oral stat. Dexamethasone 8 mg twice daily orally.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A patient receiving radical radiotherapy for head and neck cancer is prescribed a treatment course of 35 fractions over seven weeks. What is the fundamental biological rationale for delivering radiation in multiple small daily fractions rather than a single large dose?
options: To decrease the total amount of ionizing radiation used
To allow the tumor to become more hypoxic and sensitive
To exploit the better recovery capacity of normal cells
To promote the rapid development of tumor angiogenesis
To avoid the formation of free radicals in healthy tissue
correctOption: To exploit the better recovery capacity of normal cells
optionExplanations: Fractionation often allows for a higher 'total' dose to be delivered safely, not a lower amount.
Hypoxia actually makes tumors more resistant to radiation, not more sensitive.
Fractionation relies on the fact that normal cells repair DNA damage more efficiently than cancer cells between doses.
Radiation aims to destroy tumors and their vessels; promoting angiogenesis would be counterproductive to treatment goals.
Free radicals are the mechanism of damage; fractionation does not prevent their formation but allows for repair of the damage they cause.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): This allows normal cells to recover from radiation damage but recovery occurs to a lesser degree in malignant cells. Fractionation regimens vary depending on the tumour being treated.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: In the management of breast cancer, which specific immunohistochemical marker is standardly assessed to determine if the tumor is likely to respond to hormonal manipulation therapies like Tamoxifen?
optionExplanations: CEA is a general tumor marker used primarily in colorectal cancer for monitoring, not for guiding hormone therapy.
HER2 positivity indicates eligibility for targeted therapies like trastuzumab, not standard hormonal manipulation.
The presence of Oestrogen Receptors (ER) is the primary predictor of a tumor's response to hormone-blocking drugs.
CD20 is a marker for B-cell lymphomas and is the target for rituximab, an immunotherapy agent.
PSA is used for monitoring prostate cancer, not for determining hormone sensitivity in breast cancer.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 147 (Book Page): Approximately 80% of breast tumours are positive for expression of the oestrogen receptor (ER) ... indicate that the cancer may be sensitive to hormonal manipulation.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Definition and intent of Adjuvant Therapy
statement: A 45-year-old woman undergoes a successful lumpectomy for a 1.5 cm breast carcinoma. Following surgery, her oncology team decides to start a course of systemic treatment specifically designed to eradicate any remaining micrometastatic disease and reduce the risk of recurrence. Which of the following terms correctly identifies this therapeutic approach?
options: Radical therapy used as the primary modality
Neoadjuvant therapy intended for tumor shrinkage
Salvage therapy used after treatment failure
optionExplanations: Radical therapy refers to the primary treatment modality used with curative intent, which in this case was the surgery itself.
Neoadjuvant therapy is administered before the primary curative intervention, such as surgery, to downstage the tumor.
Adjuvant therapy is specifically defined as additional treatment provided after the primary surgery to eliminate residual micrometastases.
Salvage therapy is a treatment given when the primary or standard treatments have failed to control the disease.
Palliative therapy is used for incurable or metastatic disease where the goal is symptom control rather than eradication of micrometastases.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Adjuvant therapy is additional therapy given after the primary curative intervention to lower the risk of disease recurrence. Radiotherapy and/or systemic anti-cancer therapy may be given after surgery with the intention of eradicating any micrometastatic disease that remains.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Indirect mechanism of radiotherapy via free radicals
statement: Radiotherapy is a cornerstone of cancer management, utilizing ionizing radiation to induce tumor cell death. While some damage occurs through direct interaction with DNA, a significant portion of cell death is achieved through indirect mechanisms. Which of the following best describes this indirect mechanism of action?
options: Stabilizing microtubule polymers during the M phase
Inducing irreversible cross-linking of DNA strands
Competitive inhibition of topoisomerase II enzymes
Direct cleavage of the DNA phosphodiester backbone
Triggering the formation of reactive free radicals
correctOption: Triggering the formation of reactive free radicals
optionExplanations: Stabilizing microtubules is the mechanism of taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), which targets the mitotic spindle during cell division.
DNA cross-linking is the primary mechanism of alkylating agents and platinum-based chemotherapy drugs.
This is the mechanism of action for certain chemotherapy drugs like etoposide, not ionizing radiation.
This describes a direct mechanism where radiation directly breaks the physical structure of the DNA molecule.
The indirect effect of radiotherapy occurs when ionizing radiation interacts with other molecules (like water) to create free radicals that then damage DNA.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Ionising radiation kills cancer cells by two mechanisms; directly damaging cancer DNA or indirectly by triggering the formation of very reactive molecules (free radicals) that also damage cancer DNA.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Targeted anti-cancer therapies are broadly classified into monoclonal antibodies and small molecule inhibitors. These agents differ significantly in their chemical structure and their physical site of action. What is the defining characteristic that distinguishes small molecule inhibitors (the -ib family) from monoclonal antibodies?
options: They require intravenous infusion for administration
They consist of large, complex protein structures
They trigger an antibody-dependent cellular toxicity
They are small enough to enter the cancer cells
They exclusively target extracellular growth receptors
correctOption: They are small enough to enter the cancer cells
optionExplanations: -mabs usually require IV administration due to their protein nature, whereas many -ibs are available as oral formulations because of their small size.
Monoclonal antibodies are large protein structures; small molecule inhibitors are much smaller chemical compounds.
This is a function of monoclonal antibodies, which can recruit the immune system to attack the cancer cell.
The 'small molecule' designation refers to their ability to cross the cell membrane and interact with intracellular targets like tyrosine kinases.
Monoclonal antibodies (-mabs) typically target receptors overexpressed on the outside of the cell; small molecules target internal processes.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 147 (Book Page): Targeted therapies are broadly divided into two groups: monoclonal antibodies (-mab) and small molecule inhibitors (-ib). ... The -ib family typically target processes within the cell, such as the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase, and are designed to be small enough to enter the cell.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Surgical priority in Malignant Spinal Cord Compression
statement: A 62-year-old male with known metastatic prostate cancer presents to the hospital with a 3-day history of worsening thoracic back pain that he describes as 'band-like' around his chest. On examination, he has 3/5 power in both lower limbs, increased knee reflexes, and a sensory level at T10. MRI confirms a single-site compression of the spinal cord by a vertebral body mass. He is otherwise fit with a good performance status. What is the most appropriate primary management strategy to achieve the best functional outcome?
options: Palliative care referral for end-of-life pain management
Conservative management with bed rest and analgesia
Immediate initiation of high-dose radiotherapy alone
Systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy without local therapy
optionExplanations: The patient is fit and has an acute, treatable complication; palliative care for end-of-life is premature at this stage of emergency management.
Conservative management is inappropriate for an oncological emergency that causes progressive neurological deficits like MSCC.
Radiotherapy is used if surgery is not possible or for certain radiosensitive tumors, but surgery has been shown to be superior for functional recovery.
In fit patients with single-level cord compression, urgent surgery provides the best chance of preserving or regaining mobility compared to other modalities.
Chemotherapy is too slow to treat the acute mechanical compression and is not the primary emergency management for MSCC.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 140 (Book Page): Neurosurgical intervention produces superior outcomes and survival compared to radiotherapy alone, and should be considered first for all patients. It is the preferred treatment if there is a single site of disease, low volume metastatic disease, if a biopsy is required to make a diagnosis or if it is a treatable cancer.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide are widely used in chemotherapy regimens for various malignancies. Which of the following best describes the specific pharmacological mechanism by which these drugs inhibit cancer cell proliferation?
options: Formation of covalent cross-links between DNA
Prevention of the re-ligation of DNA strand breaks
Inhibition of the dihydrofolate reductase enzyme
Binding to tubulin to block microtubule formation
Incorporation into DNA leading to irreparable errors
correctOption: Formation of covalent cross-links between DNA
optionExplanations: Alkylating agents work by adding alkyl groups to DNA, resulting in covalent cross-links that prevent DNA replication and transcription.
This describes the mechanism of topoisomerase inhibitors like etoposide or irinotecan.
This is the mechanism of antifolates like methotrexate.
This is the mechanism of vinca alkaloids (e.g., vincristine).
This is the mechanism of nucleoside analogues like gemcitabine or fludarabine.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 146 (Book Page): Alkylating agents: Cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide. Mechanism of action: Form covalent cross-links between DNA molecules by adding an alkyl group to DNA.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status scale is a critical tool for clinicians to assess a patient's fitness for aggressive anti-cancer therapy. Which of the following descriptions matches a patient assigned to ECOG Grade 2?
options: Capable of only limited self-care and bedbound >50% of time
Fully active and able to carry on all usual activities
Completely disabled and confined totally to a bed or chair
Restricted in strenuous activity but able to do light work
Ambulatory and capable of self-care but unable to work
correctOption: Ambulatory and capable of self-care but unable to work
optionExplanations: This describes ECOG Grade 3.
This describes ECOG Grade 0.
This describes ECOG Grade 4.
This describes ECOG Grade 1.
Grade 2 defines a patient who can care for themselves and walk but cannot work, spending more than half their day out of bed.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 137 (Book Page): 2 Ambulatory and capable of all self-care but unable to work. Up and about more than 50% of waking hours

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Purpose and benefits of Neoadjuvant Therapy
statement: A patient with locally advanced rectal cancer is presented at a multidisciplinary team meeting. The surgical oncologist suggests a course of 'downstaging' therapy prior to the definitive resection. What is a principal advantage of this neoadjuvant approach in the management of solid tumors?
options: It increases the likelihood of successful debulking
It avoids the risk of treatment-related side effects
It eliminates the need for any surgical intervention
It relies solely on radiotherapy to cure the malignancy
It is used primarily when the patient is unfit for surgery
correctOption: It increases the likelihood of successful debulking
optionExplanations: By shrinking the tumor (downstaging), neoadjuvant therapy makes surgery more likely to be successful and may allow for less mutilating procedures.
All anti-cancer therapies, including neoadjuvant ones, carry a risk of toxicity and side effects.
Neoadjuvant therapy is given *prior* to surgery, not to replace it in curative intent cases.
Neoadjuvant therapy can be chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or both, but it is preparatory to a primary curative intervention (usually surgery).
If a patient is completely unfit for surgery, they usually receive palliative care, not neoadjuvant therapy aimed at subsequent surgery.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Neoadjuvant therapy is additional therapy given prior to the primary curative intervention. ... Any reduction in the volume of disease, or ‘downstaging’, may also allow less extensive surgery, increase the likelihood of successful debulking and improve subsequent surgical morbidity.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Palliative Care focus in poor-prognosis MUO
statement: A 78-year-old man is hospitalized with a 2-month history of significant weight loss, jaundice, and severe fatigue. Diagnostic imaging shows bulky, multi-organ metastases in the liver and bones, but no primary tumor is identified. He has a poor performance status (ECOG 4), low albumin, and high inflammatory markers. He states he does not want aggressive treatment. What is the most appropriate management according to board standards for metastatic malignant disease of undefined origin (MUO)?
options: Request urgent surgical resection of the largest metastasis
Perform multiple endoscopies to locate the primary site
Enroll the patient in a Phase I clinical trial for new drugs
Prioritize honest palliative and end-of-life care planning
correctOption: Prioritize honest palliative and end-of-life care planning
optionExplanations: Surgery is rarely curative for multi-organ metastatic disease and would likely increase morbidity in this frail patient.
Extensive 'hunting' for a primary is not indicated in patients with very poor prognosis and poor performance status.
Phase I trials are for patients with good performance status where no standard treatment exists; this patient's PS excludes him from such trials.
In MUO with multiple poor prognostic features (bulky disease, low albumin, poor PS), focusing on comfort and quality of life is the standard of care.
Aggressive chemotherapy is poorly tolerated and generally ineffective in patients with an ECOG performance status of 4.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 111 (Book Page): Patients who present as emergencies to hospital with symptomatic new metastatic cancer often have a short prognosis. Features associated with poor prognosis... include: poor performance status (PS 3–4), requirement for hospital admission, bulky or multi-organ metastatic disease... Further investigations, including biopsy, may not be warranted and honest conversations about palliative care and end-of-life planning are often preferable.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Biochemical profile of Tumor Lysis Syndrome
statement: A patient with a high-grade, bulky lymphoma is started on intensive cytotoxic chemotherapy. Within 48 hours, the clinical team monitors for Tumor Lysis Syndrome. Which of the following sets of biochemical disturbances accurately reflects the metabolic sequelae of rapid cellular destruction in this syndrome?
optionExplanations: TLS is characterized by hyperuricemia (from nucleic acids) and hypocalcemia.
Cell lysis releases intracellular ions (potassium, phosphate) and nucleic acids (leading to high uric acid). Elevated phosphate then causes calcium to drop (hypocalcemia).
Phosphate is increased in TLS, not decreased.
TLS causes hyperphosphatemia and hyperkalemia, not the reverse.
Sodium is not typically the primary electrolyte affected in TLS; hypercalcemia is not a feature (hypocalcemia is).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 142 (Book Page): Cellular destruction results in the release of potassium, phosphate, nucleic acids and purines that can cause transient hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and hyperkalaemia.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: During the course of cancer treatment, various cytotoxic agents are associated with distinct organ-specific toxicities. A patient receiving chemotherapy for lymphoma develops acute paralytic ileus. Which class of drugs is most characteristically associated with this specific gastrointestinal complication?
optionExplanations: Anthracyclines are most notable for their potential to cause cardiomyopathy and alopecia.
Vinca alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine) are notorious for neurotoxicity, which can manifest as autonomic neuropathy leading to paralytic ileus.
5-FU is commonly associated with diarrhea, stomatitis, and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia.
Taxanes are primarily associated with peripheral neuropathy and arthralgia/myalgia.
Platinum agents are more famously associated with nephrotoxicity and hearing loss.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): GI tract ... Paralytic ileus – vinca alkaloids

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A 52-year-old woman undergoes a successful wide local excision and axillary lymph node clearance for a T2N1M0 invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast. Following the primary surgical intervention, she is scheduled to begin a course of systemic therapy to eliminate potential micrometastatic disease and reduce the risk of future recurrence. How is this specific timing and intent of therapy classified?
options: Salvage therapy intended for refractory disease
Radical therapy intended for local remission
Adjuvant therapy intended for risk reduction
Palliative therapy intended for symptom control
correctOption: Adjuvant therapy intended for risk reduction
optionExplanations: Salvage therapy is used after the failure of standard initial treatments, not as a scheduled post-operative risk reduction measure.
Radical therapy refers to the primary treatment (like surgery or radiation) given with curative intent to the main tumour site.
Adjuvant therapy specifically refers to treatment given after the primary intervention (like surgery) to target potential micrometastases.
Neoadjuvant therapy is administered prior to the primary curative intervention, not after.
Palliative therapy is used when cure is not possible, aiming to control symptoms rather than eliminate micrometastatic risk in a curative setting.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Adjuvant therapy is additional therapy given after the primary curative intervention to lower the risk of disease recurrence. Radiotherapy and/or systemic anti-cancer therapy may be given after surgery with the intention of eradicating any micrometastatic disease that remains.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Ionising radiation in clinical oncology utilizes various mechanisms to achieve cellular destruction. While direct damage to cancer DNA occurs, a significant portion of the therapeutic effect is mediated by the indirect action of radiation. What is the primary mechanism involved in this indirect DNA damage?
options: Triggering the formation of free radicals
Activation of the caspase proteolytic cascade
Inhibition of the topoisomerase I enzyme
correctOption: Triggering the formation of free radicals
optionExplanations: Indirect damage occurs when radiation interacts with water or other molecules to produce free radicals, which then react with and damage DNA.
Microtubule stabilization is the mechanism of taxane chemotherapy drugs.
While apoptosis (caspase activation) is the final outcome, it is not the primary 'indirect action' mechanism described for radiation interaction.
Growth receptor blockade is the mechanism of targeted monoclonal antibodies or small molecule inhibitors.
Topoisomerase inhibition is a mechanism used by certain chemotherapy agents, not ionising radiation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Ionising radiation kills cancer cells by two mechanisms; directly damaging cancer DNA or indirectly by triggering the formation of very reactive molecules (free radicals) that also damage cancer DNA.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Targeted anti-cancer therapies are broadly classified based on their chemical structure and the cellular location of their targets. A drug that is designed to be small enough to enter the cell and inhibit processes such as the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase typically follows which nomenclature convention?
optionExplanations: -ine is common for many drugs (e.g., vincristine) but is not the specific suffix for targeted small molecule inhibitors in modern nomenclature classification used to differentiate them from monoclonal antibodies.
-abine is common for nucleoside analogues (antimetabolites) like gemcitabine.
-ib agents are small molecule inhibitors capable of intracellular penetration to target signalling pathways.
-amide is common in alkylating agents like cyclophosphamide but does not specifically denote a targeted small molecule inhibitor.
-mab agents are monoclonal antibodies that typically target proteins on the outside of the cell.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 147 (Book Page): Targeted therapies are broadly divided into two groups: monoclonal antibodies (-mab) and small molecule inhibitors (-ib). ... The -ib family typically target processes within the cell, such as the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase, and are designed to be small enough to enter the cell.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Management of Metastatic Cancer of Undefined Primary (MUO)
statement: A 78-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history is admitted following a fall. Evaluation reveals icterus, abdominal distension with positive fluid thrill, and cachexia. Laboratory studies show a haemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, elevated C-reactive protein, and hypoalbuminaemia. A computed tomography (CT) scan identifies multiple lesions in the liver, both lungs, and lytic lesions in the lumbar spine, but no clear primary site. The patient is largely bed-bound, requiring assistance for all self-care, and spends most of the day sleeping. What is the most appropriate management approach for this patient?
options: Radical radiotherapy to the spinal lesions
optionExplanations: Radical radiotherapy is intended for cure; while palliative radiation might help pain, the overall management must be holistic end-of-life care given the systemic disease burden and frailty.
Given the poor performance status (ECOG 3-4), multi-organ involvement, and adverse laboratory markers, the focus should shift to palliative care as survival is very short.
Invasive biopsies in a patient with PS 3-4 and poor prognostic markers often provide little clinical benefit and may not be in the patient's best interest.
While supportive, TPN does not address the underlying advanced malignancy and does not change the poor prognosis in cachectic cancer patients.
Systemic chemotherapy is generally poorly tolerated and ineffective in patients with extremely low performance status and bulky MUO.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 111 (Book Page): Features associated with poor prognosis... include: poor performance status (PS 3–4), requirement for hospital admission, bulky or multi-organ metastatic disease... raised inflammatory markers and low albumin. Further investigations, including biopsy, may not be warranted and honest conversations about palliative care and end-of-life planning are often preferable.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Cytotoxic chemotherapy agents like Epirubicin and Doxorubicin belong to the anthracycline class. According to their primary mechanism of action, how do these specific drugs interfere with the cell's ability to proliferate?
options: By binding to tubulin and blocking microtubule formation
By forming covalent cross-links between DNA molecules
By stabilizing the microtubule polymer preventing disassembly
By intercalating with DNA and inhibiting topoisomerase II
By inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase to stop purine synthesis
correctOption: By intercalating with DNA and inhibiting topoisomerase II
optionExplanations: This is the mechanism of vinca alkaloids (e.g., vincristine).
This is the mechanism of nitrogen mustards and other alkylating agents.
This is the mechanism of taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel).
Anthracyclines work by intercalating between DNA base pairs and inhibiting Topoisomerase II, leading to DNA damage.
This is the mechanism of antifolates (e.g., methotrexate).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 146 (Book Page): Fig. 7.10 ... Anthracyclines: epirubicin, doxorubicin ... Mechanism of action: Intercalate with DNA and inhibit the progression of topoisomerase II.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: In the surgical management of metastatic disease, procedures are frequently utilized for symptom relief rather than cure. What clinical term is used for a surgical intervention performed specifically to manage and clean fungating skin lesions in advanced cancer?
optionExplanations: Neoadjuvant is not a surgical term; it refers to therapy given before surgery.
Sentinel surgery usually refers to sentinel lymph node biopsy, which is a diagnostic/staging procedure.
Debulking refers to removing as much of the primary tumor as possible, often in ovarian cancer.
Toilet surgery is the specific clinical term for cleaning and debriding fungating, malodorous, or infected tumor lesions for palliative hygiene.
Cytoreductive surgery is another term for debulking, aimed at reducing tumor burden to improve survival or response to other therapies.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Examples [of surgical palliation] include ... the treatment of fungating skin lesions by ‘toilet’ surgery.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: During the planning of radical radiotherapy, the total radiation dose is typically divided into multiple small doses delivered over several weeks. What is the fundamental biological rationale for this practice, known as fractionation?
options: It prevents the activation of the 'angiogenic switch' in the tumour bed
It allows normal cells to recover from damage better than malignant cells
It ensures that oxygen levels in the tumour remain high for radical production
It synchronizes all cancer cells into the more radiosensitive G0 phase
It stimulates the immune system to produce more reactive oxygen species
correctOption: It allows normal cells to recover from damage better than malignant cells
optionExplanations: Fractionation is not primarily designed to stop the angiogenic switch.
Fractionation exploits the fact that normal tissues have more effective DNA repair mechanisms and can recover between doses better than cancer cells.
Tumour reoxygenation is a factor in fractionation, but the primary therapeutic benefit cited is the differential recovery rate.
Cancer cells in G0 are generally more radioresistant, not more sensitive; the cell cycle effect of fractionation involves reassortment into sensitive phases (M/G2).
While radiation produces reactive oxygen species, the goal of fractionation is not to stimulate the immune system to produce them.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Biological differences between normal and tumour tissues are exploited to obtain therapeutic benefit. Fundamental to this is fractionation... This allows normal cells to recover from radiation damage but recovery occurs to a lesser degree in malignant cells.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Management of Malignant Spinal Cord Compression
statement: A 64-year-old female with a history of stage IV breast cancer presents with progressively worsening back pain over two weeks. The pain is described as a 'band-like' sensation around her thorax and is significantly aggravated when she lies flat or coughs. Physical examination reveals symmetrical lower limb weakness (Grade 3/5 power), increased knee jerks, and an extensor plantar response bilaterally. An urgent MRI confirms a single-level vertebral body mass causing significant spinal cord compression at T6. Her performance status is ECOG 2. What is the preferred first-line definitive treatment to achieve superior outcomes in this patient?
optionExplanations: Neurosurgery followed by radiotherapy provides better functional outcomes (ambulation) in patients with single-level spinal cord compression compared to radiation alone.
Radiotherapy is used for patients not fit for surgery or with multiple sites, but neurosurgery has been shown to have superior outcomes in single-site compression.
Bisphosphonates prevent future skeletal events but do not decompress the spinal cord in an acute emergency.
Chemotherapy is too slow to prevent permanent neurological damage in an acute cord compression emergency.
Observation is inappropriate as establish neurological deficits like paraplegia are often irreversible if not treated urgently.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 140 (Book Page): Neurosurgical intervention produces superior outcomes and survival compared to radiotherapy alone, and should be considered first for all patients. It is the preferred treatment if there is a single site of disease...

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Mechanism of Hormonal Therapy in Prostate Cancer
statement: In the management of advanced prostate cancer, hormonal manipulation is a standard strategy to control disease growth. Medications such as Goserelin are frequently used to achieve this. What is the primary mechanism by which these drugs exert their effect?
options: Reduction of systemic androgen levels via LHRH antagonism
Competitive inhibition of the aromatase enzyme in fatty tissue
Induction of apoptosis by mimicking cytotoxic steroid action
Direct inhibition of the intracellular tyrosine kinase cascade
Blockade of androgen receptors on the tumour cell surface
correctOption: Reduction of systemic androgen levels via LHRH antagonism
optionExplanations: Goserelin is an LHRH analogue that ultimately leads to the suppression of testicular testosterone production, reducing systemic androgen levels.
Aromatase inhibitors are used in breast cancer to reduce oestrogen levels, not in prostate cancer management.
Glucocorticoids (steroids) can induce apoptosis in some lymphoid cancers, but this is not the mechanism of LHRH analogues in prostate cancer.
This describes targeted small molecule inhibitors, not hormonal therapy.
This is the mechanism of anti-androgens like bicalutamide, not LHRH analogues like goserelin.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 147 (Book Page): In prostate cancer, hormonal therapy (e.g. luteinising hormone releasing hormone (LHRH) analogues such as goserelin... aimed at reducing androgen levels can provide good long-term control of advanced disease.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A 68-year-old male with localized prostate cancer is scheduled for a treatment that involves the permanent placement of small radioactive seeds directly into the prostate gland. This technique allows for the delivery of high-dose radiation locally while sparing surrounding healthy tissues. What is the correct term for this modality of treatment?
optionExplanations: Stereotactic radiotherapy uses many focused external beams converging on a point; it is not internal.
Proton therapy uses high-energy protons from a cyclotron (external) rather than implanted seeds.
External beam radiotherapy delivers radiation from a source outside the body (e.g., linear accelerator).
Intensity modulated radiotherapy is a form of advanced external beam therapy.
Brachytherapy involves placing the radioactive source directly inside or on the surface of the tumor.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Brachytherapy, or internal radiation therapy, involves the direct application of a radioactive source onto or into a tumour. ... In other cases, such as in prostate cancer, small radioactive seeds may be permanently placed, releasing radiation slowly over several months.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Primary Curative Modality in Solid Tumors
statement: In the multimodal management of solid organ malignancies, what is primarily considered the most frequent and pivotal curative intervention for early-stage localized disease?
options: Surgical resection of all macroscopic disease
correctOption: Surgical resection of all macroscopic disease
optionExplanations: Brachytherapy is a localized treatment for specific sites like the prostate but is not the most frequent primary curative intervention overall.
Chemotherapy is often used as adjuvant or primary treatment for non-solid tumors (like lymphoma) but is not the primary curative step for most solid cancers.
Immunotherapy is predominantly used in metastatic settings or as adjuvant therapy in specific cases, not as the primary curative macroscopic intervention.
Radiotherapy can be used with radical intent but is statistically less frequent as the primary curative step compared to surgical resection.
Correct. Surgery is the mainstay for curing early localized solid cancers like colorectal, breast, and lung cancer.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): [Surgery to remove all macroscopic disease is most frequently the primary curative intervention.]

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Radiation therapy induces the death of cancer cells through complex molecular pathways. Which mechanism describes the indirect cytotoxic effect of ionizing radiation on cellular DNA?
options: Inhibition of the religation step by topoisomerase enzymes
Intercalation between base pairs to prevent transcription
Covalent attachment of alkyl groups to guanine bases
Induction of reactive molecules known as free radicals
Permanent stabilization of the microtubule polymer structure
correctOption: Induction of reactive molecules known as free radicals
optionExplanations: This describes the mechanism of topoisomerase inhibitors, a class of systemic chemotherapy.
This is the mechanism for certain antitumour antibiotics like anthracyclines.
This describes the mechanism of alkylating agents in chemotherapy, not ionizing radiation.
Correct. Ionizing radiation indirectly damages DNA by producing free radicals that cause lethal genomic lesions.
This describes the mechanism of taxanes, which interfere with microtubule disassembly during mitosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): [Ionising radiation kills cancer cells by two mechanisms; directly damaging cancer DNA or indirectly by triggering the formation of very reactive molecules (free radicals) that also damage cancer DNA.]

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A patient with locally advanced esophageal cancer is scheduled for systemic anti-cancer therapy prior to his definitive surgical intervention. What is the primary clinical objective of this specific treatment sequence?
options: To increase the likelihood of achieving surgical debulking
To replace the need for postoperative adjuvant radiotherapy
To provide symptom control in an incurable metastatic setting
To minimize the duration of the subsequent hospital admission
To treat microscopic disease remaining after primary resection
correctOption: To increase the likelihood of achieving surgical debulking
optionExplanations: Correct. Neoadjuvant therapy aims to downstage the tumor, facilitating a more effective or less invasive surgical procedure.
Neoadjuvant therapy does not automatically replace the potential need for postoperative treatments.
This describes palliative therapy, which is not intended for curative downstaging before surgery.
The goal is clinical outcome (recurrence risk and surgical success) rather than the administrative duration of hospital stay.
This describes the goal of adjuvant therapy, which is given after the primary intervention.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): [Neoadjuvant therapy is additional therapy given prior to the primary curative intervention. ... any reduction in the volume of disease, or ‘downstaging’, may also allow less extensive surgery, increase the likelihood of successful debulking and improve subsequent surgical morbidity.]

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Management of Metastatic Malignancy with Poor Prognosis
statement: A 74-year-old male with a 50 pack-year smoking history is admitted through the emergency department with a two-week history of significant weight loss, early satiety, and progressive dyspnea. Initial CT imaging reveals bulky, multi-organ metastatic disease involving the liver, lungs, and thoracic vertebrae, with no identifiable primary site. Laboratory results show a low serum albumin, elevated C-reactive protein, and significantly raised lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). He requires assistance for all self-care and spends more than 50% of his waking hours in bed. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: Initiation of high-dose combination cytotoxic chemotherapy
Prioritization of palliative care and end-of-life planning
Comprehensive endoscopic evaluation including colonoscopy and EGD
Immediate referral for surgical resection of the largest metastasis
Urgent biopsy of the liver via ultrasound-guided intervention
correctOption: Prioritization of palliative care and end-of-life planning
optionExplanations: Chemotherapy is unlikely to be tolerated or beneficial in a patient with PS 3 and multi-organ failure signs.
Correct. The combination of high PS (likely ECOG 3), multi-organ spread, and biochemical markers (raised LDH/CRP, low albumin) indicates a very poor prognosis where palliative care is prioritized.
Extensive 'hunting' for the primary site is often not warranted in patients with multiple poor prognostic markers and high PS scores.
Surgery is rarely curative in multi-organ metastatic disease, especially in a patient with poor performance status.
While biopsy establishes diagnosis, the clinical status here suggests that aggressive diagnostic pursuits may not be in the patient's best interest.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 139 (Book Page): [Features associated with poor prognosis, irrespective of subsequent diagnosis, include: poor performance status (PS 3–4), requirement for hospital admission, bulky or multi-organ metastatic disease, significant comorbidity, raised LDH, raised inflammatory markers and low albumin. Further investigations, including biopsy, may not be warranted and honest conversations about palliative care and end-of-life planning are often preferable.]

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: While both platinum-based agents and nitrogen mustards are used in systemic cancer treatment, they differ in their specific chemical interaction with DNA. What distinguishes the mechanism of nitrogen mustards from that of platinum agents?
options: The covalent addition of an alkyl group to the DNA molecule
The prevention of tubulin polymerization into functional microtubules
The reversible binding to DNA to inhibit ribosomal transcription
The inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase to stop purine synthesis
The formation of intra-strand cross-links without adding alkyl groups
correctOption: The covalent addition of an alkyl group to the DNA molecule
optionExplanations: Correct. Nitrogen mustards (like cyclophosphamide) are true alkylating agents that covalently add alkyl groups.
This describes the mechanism of mitotic inhibitors like vinca alkaloids.
This is not the mechanism for either class; both cause more permanent DNA damage/cross-linking.
This describes the mechanism of antifolates like methotrexate.
This describes the mechanism of platinum agents (alkylating-like), not nitrogen mustards.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 146 (Book Page): [Nitrogen mustards: Form covalent cross-links between DNA molecules by adding an alkyl group to DNA. ... Platinum agents: Form inter-/intra-strand cross-links between DNA molecules, not by adding an alkyl group, so considered alkylating-like agents.]

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: During the radiological evaluation of a patient's response to systemic anti-cancer therapy using the RECIST criteria, how is 'Stable Disease' defined?
options: A decrease of at least 30% in the sum of the longest diameters
The appearance of one or more completely new malignant lesions
An increase of at least 20% in the sum of the longest diameters
Insufficient shrinkage for partial response and insufficient growth for progression
Disappearance of all previously identified target lesions
correctOption: Insufficient shrinkage for partial response and insufficient growth for progression
optionExplanations: This is the definition of Partial Response (PR).
This also qualifies as Progressive Disease (PD).
This is part of the definition for Progressive Disease (PD).
Correct. Stable disease indicates the tumor size has not changed significantly enough to meet criteria for response or progression.
This is the definition of Complete Response (CR).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 148 (Book Page): [Stable disease (SD): Neither sufficient shrinkage to qualify for PR nor sufficient increase to qualify for PD, taking as reference the smallest sum LD since the treatment started.]

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A radiation oncologist explains the rationale for delivering radiation as multiple small daily doses over several weeks rather than a single large dose. What biological principle justifies this fractionation regimen?
options: It facilitates the synchronization of the cell cycle into the G0 phase
It maximizes the accumulation of free radicals in the intracellular space
It prevents the activation of cellular autophagy in stressed cancer cells
It ensures the delivery of a higher cumulative dose to healthy tissue
It allows normal cells to recover more effectively than malignant cells
correctOption: It allows normal cells to recover more effectively than malignant cells
optionExplanations: Radiation tends to cause arrest at checkpoints (G1/S or G2/M), not necessarily synchronization into the quiescent G0 phase.
Free radical formation occurs with each dose but is not the primary rationale for the timing of fractionation.
Autophagy is actually a cytoprotective mechanism induced by radiation, not prevented by fractionation.
Fractionation is intended to spare healthy tissue, not deliver a higher dose to it.
Correct. Fractionation exploits the superior repair capacity of normal tissues compared to malignant tissues.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): [Fundamental to this is fractionation, which entails delivering the radiation as a number of small doses on a daily basis. This allows normal cells to recover from radiation damage but recovery occurs to a lesser degree in malignant cells.]

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A 62-year-old female with known metastatic breast cancer involving the ribs and pelvis presents to the clinic with a 'band-like' pain across her mid-thoracic region that worsens when she lies flat. On physical examination, there is increased tone in the lower limbs, brisk knee reflexes, and extensor plantar responses. She reports that she had difficulty initiating urination this morning. What is the most immediate priority in the medical management of this oncological emergency?
options: Initiate urgent whole-brain radiotherapy for symptom control
Perform an urgent isotope bone scan to identify new lesions
Schedule elective surgical stabilization of the spinal column
Administer high-dose intravenous or oral dexamethasone
Start intravenous bisphosphonate therapy to reduce bone pain
correctOption: Administer high-dose intravenous or oral dexamethasone
optionExplanations: The symptoms (thoracic band pain, UMN signs in lower limbs) point to spinal compression, not brain involvement.
MRI is the preferred imaging; an isotope bone scan is not sufficient to diagnose spinal cord compression.
Surgery is a definitive option but high-dose steroids must be given immediately upon suspicion to reduce edema.
Correct. Immediate administration of high-dose steroids (dexamethasone) is the standard priority for suspected malignant spinal cord compression.
Bisphosphonates are for hypercalcemia or long-term bone health, not for acute cord compression.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 140 (Book Page): [Malignant spinal cord compression is a medical emergency and should be treated with analgesia and high-dose glucocorticoid therapy (Box 7.14). ... Administer high-dose glucocorticoids: Dexamethasone 16 mg IV or oral stat; Dexamethasone 8 mg twice daily orally.]

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Role of Debulking Surgery in Cancer
statement: In patients with advanced-stage ovarian carcinoma, the surgical approach often differs from that of other localized solid tumors. What term describes the surgical goal of removing as much of the tumor mass as possible to improve the efficacy of subsequent chemotherapy?
options: Wide local excision with negative margins
Sentinel lymph node mapping and biopsy
optionExplanations: Neoadjuvant refers to therapy given before surgery, not the surgical procedure itself.
Prophylactic surgery is performed before cancer develops (e.g., in BRCA mutation carriers).
This is the goal for early localized tumors (like breast or melanoma) where margins are the priority.
Correct. Cytoreductive (debulking) surgery is used in advanced ovarian cancer to reduce tumor burden and enhance chemotherapy effectiveness.
Sentinel node mapping is a staging technique, not a therapeutic mass-removal strategy.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): [Debulking cytoreductive surgery may improve survival in some cancers, including renal cell carcinoma and ovarian cancer.] Page 150 (Book Page): [Even in advanced disease, surgery is undertaken to maximally debulk the tumour and is followed by cytotoxic chemotherapy.]

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A patient undergoing curative-intent treatment for lymphoma receives a chemotherapy regimen containing anthracyclines (such as doxorubicin). Which late-onset systemic toxicity must the clinical team specifically monitor for in the years following completion of therapy?
optionExplanations: Correct. Anthracyclines are well-known for causing dose-dependent cardiotoxicity and late-onset heart failure.
Hand-foot syndrome (erythrodysesthesia) is common with 5-FU and capecitabine.
Hemorrhagic cystitis is a specific toxicity of ifosfamide and cyclophosphamide.
Hearing loss is a specific toxicity associated with cisplatin, not anthracyclines.
Paralytic ileus is an acute toxicity associated with vinca alkaloids.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 149 (Book Page): [Late consequences of cytotoxic chemotherapy include heart failure due to cardiotoxicity, pulmonary fibrosis, nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.] Page 129 (Book Page): [Cardiomyopathy – HER2 inhibitors, anthracyclines, radiotherapy.]

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Which term best describes systemic anti-cancer therapy administered after a primary surgical resection to eradicate residual micrometastatic disease and reduce the risk of tumor recurrence?
optionExplanations: Neoadjuvant therapy is administered prior to the primary curative intervention, often to downstage a tumor before surgery.
Salvage therapy is treatment given after a cancer has failed to respond to other treatments or has recurred after a period of remission.
Radical therapy refers to the primary treatment given with curative intent, such as radical radiotherapy or radical surgery.
Adjuvant therapy is specifically defined as treatment given after the main intervention (like surgery) to target potential remaining microscopic disease.
Palliative therapy is primarily used to treat patients with metastatic disease where curative treatment is not possible, focusing on quality of life and symptom control.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Adjuvant therapy is additional therapy given after the primary curative intervention to lower the risk of disease recurrence. Radiotherapy and/or systemic anti-cancer therapy may be given after surgery with the intention of eradicating any micrometastatic disease that remains.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Ionizing radiation destroys malignant cells through both direct and indirect pathways. Which of the following describes the indirect mechanism of radiotherapy-induced cell death?
options: Formation of reactive free radicals that damage the cancer DNA
Direct cleavage of the double-stranded DNA phosphate backbone
Stabilization of the microtubule polymer to prevent cell disassembly
Inhibition of the topoisomerase II enzyme during DNA synthesis
Competitive binding to intracellular estrogen and steroid receptors
correctOption: Formation of reactive free radicals that damage the cancer DNA
optionExplanations: The indirect mechanism involves the radiolysis of water or other molecules to create free radicals, which then interact with and damage the DNA.
This describes the direct mechanism of radiation where the ionizing energy interacts directly with the DNA molecule.
Microtubule stabilization is the mechanism of action for taxanes, a class of cytotoxic chemotherapy drugs.
Topoisomerase II inhibition is a mechanism used by certain chemotherapy agents like etoposide, not radiotherapy.
Hormone therapy, not radiotherapy, involves blocking or binding to steroid receptors to inhibit tumor growth.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Ionising radiation kills cancer cells by two mechanisms; directly damaging cancer DNA or indirectly by triggering the formation of very reactive molecules (free radicals) that also damage cancer DNA.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Role and Benefits of Neoadjuvant Therapy
statement: A 54-year-old woman is scheduled for systemic anti-cancer therapy prior to a planned surgical resection for her breast carcinoma. What is a principal advantage of this neoadjuvant approach for the surgical management?
options: It facilitates the permanent storage of oocytes prior to radical therapy
It reduces the risk of developing acute radiotherapy-induced fibrosis
It prevents the late toxicity associated with axillary lymph node dissection
It eliminates the requirement for post-operative pathological staging
It allows for a more conservative, organ-preserving surgical procedure
correctOption: It allows for a more conservative, organ-preserving surgical procedure
optionExplanations: Fertility preservation is a separate supportive care issue that should be addressed regardless of the timing of chemotherapy.
Neoadjuvant therapy does not inherently reduce radiotherapy toxicity; these are independent treatment modalities with different side effect profiles.
Neoadjuvant therapy does not replace the need for axillary management and does not prevent the toxicity associated with lymph node surgery.
Neoadjuvant therapy does not eliminate the need for staging; rather, the surgical specimen is used to evaluate the effectiveness of the treatment.
By shrinking the tumor (downstaging), neoadjuvant therapy can convert a patient who needed a mastectomy into a candidate for breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Any reduction in the volume of disease, or ‘downstaging’, may also allow less extensive surgery, increase the likelihood of successful debulking and improve subsequent surgical morbidity.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A 78-year-old man with metastatic renal cell carcinoma is admitted with severe fatigue and confusion. He has multiple metastases in the brain and liver. He is completely bedbound and requires total assistance for all self-care. His albumin is low and inflammatory markers are significantly raised. What is the most appropriate goal of management for this patient?
options: Enrolment in a Phase I clinical trial for targeted immunotherapy
Referral for urgent radical debulking of the primary tumor
Referral to palliative care for end-of-life planning and support
Initiation of high-dose cytotoxic combination chemotherapy
Application of stereotactic radiotherapy to all metastatic sites
correctOption: Referral to palliative care for end-of-life planning and support
optionExplanations: Phase I trials are for patients with good performance status who have exhausted standard options; this patient is too frail for experimental therapy.
Radical debulking is not appropriate for a patient with PS 4 and multi-organ metastases, as they are unlikely to survive or benefit from the procedure.
The patient's advanced age, poor performance status (PS 4), multi-organ spread, and biochemical markers indicate a very limited prognosis, making palliative care the most ethical and effective focus.
Cytotoxic chemotherapy is generally avoided in patients with a performance status of 3-4 due to high toxicity and poor outcomes.
Stereotactic radiotherapy is used for solitary or limited metastases, not for widespread multi-organ disease in a terminal patient.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 111 (Book Page): Features associated with poor prognosis, irrespective of subsequent diagnosis, include: poor performance status (PS 3–4), requirement for hospital admission, bulky or multi-organ metastatic disease, significant comorbidity, raised LDH, raised inflammatory markers and low albumin. Further investigations, including biopsy, may not be warranted and honest conversations about palliative care and end-of-life planning are often preferable.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A patient undergoing cytotoxic chemotherapy for a hematological malignancy develops severe constipation, abdominal distension, and decreased bowel sounds. Which of the following drug classes is classically associated with this paralytic ileus?
optionExplanations: Platinum agents (e.g., cisplatin) are more commonly associated with nephrotoxicity, hearing loss, and severe nausea.
Anthracyclines (e.g., doxorubicin) are primarily associated with cardiomyopathy and myelosuppression.
Vinca alkaloids (e.g., vincristine) are neurotoxic and can cause autonomic neuropathy, leading to paralytic ileus.
Antifolates (e.g., methotrexate) commonly cause stomatitis, myelosuppression, and hepatotoxicity.
Taxanes are often associated with peripheral neuropathy, neutropenia, and arthralgia, rather than paralytic ileus.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): GI tract... Paralytic ileus – vinca alkaloids

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: In the evaluation of treatment response using the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), what defines a Partial Response (PR)?
options: Sufficient shrinkage of lesions to eliminate the need for surgical excision
The complete disappearance of all target and non-target lesions
At least a 10% decrease in the sum of the longest diameters of target lesions
At least a 20% increase in the sum of the longest diameters of target lesions
At least a 30% decrease in the sum of the longest diameters of target lesions
correctOption: At least a 30% decrease in the sum of the longest diameters of target lesions
optionExplanations: Surgical resectability is a clinical judgment and is not a formal criterion used in the RECIST measurement system.
This describes a Complete Response (CR), not a Partial Response.
A 10% decrease is insufficient to qualify as a Partial Response according to RECIST criteria.
A 20% increase defines Progressive Disease (PD), which is the opposite of a therapeutic response.
A 30% reduction in the sum of the longest diameters of target lesions is the standard objective threshold for PR.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 148 (Book Page): Partial response (PR): At least a 30% decrease in the sum of the longest diameter (LD) of target lesions, taking as reference the baseline sum LD.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: While surgery is often used palliatively, it can also be used as 'debulking' cytoreductive therapy to potentially improve survival in advanced disease. In which of the following malignancies is this approach most commonly established?
optionExplanations: Nasopharyngeal cancer is primarily treated with radiotherapy or chemo-radiotherapy, as the primary site is surgically difficult to access.
Metastatic melanoma is usually managed with immunotherapy or targeted therapy; surgery is reserved for solitary, symptomatic metastases.
Systemic therapy, not surgery, is the primary treatment for small cell lung cancer due to its early systemic spread.
Ovarian cancer is a classic example where aggressive surgical debulking (removing as much macroscopic tumor as possible) correlates with better survival outcomes.
High-grade neuro-endocrine tumors are mainly managed with systemic chemotherapy; surgery has a very limited role in advanced cases.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Debulking cytoreductive surgery may improve survival in some cancers, including renal cell carcinoma and ovarian cancer.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: A 66-year-old male with a history of metastatic prostate cancer presents with a 4-day history of worsening mid-thoracic back pain that feels like a 'band' around his chest. He reports that the pain is worst when he lies flat or coughs. On examination, he has increased knee reflexes and extensor plantar responses. What is the most appropriate next step in the emergency management of this patient?
options: Initiate high-dose cytotoxic chemotherapy to reduce the tumor burden in the spine
Refer the patient for immediate palliative surgery without prior imaging
Wait for 24 hours to monitor for the development of urinary retention or incontinence
Order a plain thoracic spine X-ray to check for vertebral fractures before treatment
Administer 16 mg of intravenous dexamethasone and arrange an urgent spinal MRI
correctOption: Administer 16 mg of intravenous dexamethasone and arrange an urgent spinal MRI
optionExplanations: While chemotherapy may be used later, steroids and decompression (surgery or radiotherapy) are the immediate emergency requirements.
Imaging (MRI) must be performed first to identify the level and extent of the compression before surgery or radiotherapy can be targeted.
Waiting is inappropriate; cord compression is an emergency, and delays lead to irreversible neurological deficits like paraplegia.
Plain X-rays are insufficient to diagnose cord compression or assess the soft tissue mass extension; MRI is the gold standard.
Malignant spinal cord compression is a surgical/oncological emergency. The priority is to reduce edema with steroids and confirm the site of compression via MRI to plan intervention.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 112 (Book Page): Malignant spinal cord compression is a medical emergency and should be treated with analgesia and high-dose glucocorticoid therapy (Box 7.14). Box 7.14: Management of suspected spinal cord compression... Confirm diagnosis with urgent MRI scan of whole spine... Administer high-dose glucocorticoids: Dexamethasone 16 mg IV or oral stat.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Metabolic complications of malignancy often require urgent management. What is the primary mechanism responsible for hypercalcaemia in approximately 80% of cancer cases?
options: Excessive intake of calcium secondary to paraneoplastic polydipsia
Ectopic production of parathyroid hormone (PTH) by the tumor
Reduced renal excretion of calcium due to chemotherapy-induced injury
Direct osteolysis from tumor cells invading the bone matrix
optionExplanations: Polydipsia is a symptom of hypercalcaemia (due to polyuria), not a cause of it.
PTHrP is the dominant mediator in humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy, acting on the same receptors as PTH to raise calcium.
Ectopic secretion of true PTH (parathyroid hormone) is a very rare mechanism of cancer-associated hypercalcaemia.
Chemotherapy-induced renal injury (like cisplatin) usually causes electrolyte wasting (e.g., hypomagnesemia) rather than hypercalcaemia.
Direct invasion of bone (local osteolysis) accounts for only about 20% of cases, not the majority.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 142 (Book Page): It is most commonly due to over-production of PTHrP (80%), which binds to the PTH receptor and elevates serum calcium by stimulating osteoclastic bone resorption and increasing renal tubular reabsorption of calcium.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Which of the following describes internal radiation therapy where a radioactive source is placed permanently or temporarily into a body cavity or tissue near the tumor?
optionExplanations: Stereotactic radiotherapy is a highly focused external beam technique delivering high doses from many angles.
A linear accelerator (Linac) is the machine used to generate the photon or electron beams for external radiotherapy.
IMRT is a sophisticated type of external beam radiotherapy that varies beam intensity to match tumor shape.
Proton therapy is a form of external beam therapy using high-energy protons instead of X-rays.
Brachytherapy specifically refers to placing the radiation source (like seeds or applicators) inside or on the patient's body.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Brachytherapy, or internal radiation therapy, involves the direct application of a radioactive source onto or into a tumor. This allows the delivery of a high, localised dose of radiation.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Which of the following terms best describes systemic anti-cancer therapy administered prior to a planned surgical intervention with the primary aim of reducing tumor volume and lowering the risk of disease recurrence?
optionExplanations: Adjuvant therapy is given after the primary curative intervention (like surgery) to eradicate microscopic disease.
Palliative therapy is aimed at symptom control and quality of life in metastatic or incurable disease, not downsizing for cure.
Curative or radical therapy refers to the overall goal of achieving complete remission, not a specific timing relative to surgery.
Neoadjuvant therapy is specifically defined as therapy given before the primary intervention to improve surgical outcomes and reduce recurrence risk.
Maintenance therapy is given after an initial response to keep the cancer in remission for a longer period.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Neoadjuvant therapy is additional therapy given prior to the primary curative intervention. Systemic anti-cancer therapy may be administered prior to planned surgery. The principal aim is to lower the risk of disease recurrence.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
statement: Ionizing radiation utilized in radiotherapy induces cancer cell lethality primarily through which mechanistic pathway?
options: Formation of reactive oxygen free radicals
Covalent cross-linking of adjacent DNA strands
Inhibition of the microtubule polymer assembly
correctOption: Formation of reactive oxygen free radicals
optionExplanations: Radiotherapy works by direct DNA damage or indirectly via the production of reactive free radicals that damage DNA.
Competitive blockade of estrogen receptors is the mechanism of hormonal therapies like tamoxifen.
Covalent cross-linking of DNA is the mechanism of alkylating agents and platinum-based chemotherapy.
Microtubule assembly inhibition is the mechanism of vinca alkaloids, a class of chemotherapy.
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are part of targeted therapy, not the mechanism of ionizing radiation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 145 (Book Page): Ionising radiation kills cancer cells by two mechanisms; directly damaging cancer DNA or indirectly by triggering the formation of very reactive molecules (free radicals) that also damage cancer DNA.

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Surgical Indications in Metastatic Bone Disease
statement: In the management of metastatic bone disease, which clinical finding is the most definitive indication for surgical intervention rather than palliative radiotherapy alone?
options: Severe bone pain that is most marked at night
Elevated serum alkaline phosphatase with a positive isotope scan
Presence of a lytic lesion in the axial skeleton
Hypercalcaemia of malignancy resistant to bisphosphonates
Lytic lesion in a weight-bearing bone with 60% cortical involvement
correctOption: Lytic lesion in a weight-bearing bone with 60% cortical involvement
optionExplanations: Pain, especially nocturnal pain, is common in bone metastases and is typically treated with radiotherapy or analgesics.
Elevated markers and positive scans confirm the diagnosis but do not dictate a surgical approach over other modalities.
Lytic lesions in the axial skeleton often respond well to radiotherapy; they are not an absolute surgical indication unless causing instability.
Refractory hypercalcaemia is managed with medical therapies like denosumab or fluids, not typically surgery.
Impending fractures, defined by more than 50% cortical involvement of a weight-bearing bone, require surgical stabilization to prevent collapse.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 144 (Book Page): Surgical intervention may be warranted where there is evidence of skeletal instability... or an impending fracture (e.g. a large lytic lesion on a weight-bearing bone with more than 50% cortical involvement).

category: Discuss the role of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and palliative care in cancer management
coreConcept: Management of Superior Vena Cava Obstruction (SVCO)
statement: A 58-year-old male with a 40 pack-year smoking history presents with a 3-week history of progressively worsening facial swelling, breathlessness, and a dull headache that is exacerbated by leaning forward. Physical examination reveals distended, non-pulsatile neck veins and plethora of the face. A CT scan confirms a large mediastinal mass compressing the superior vena cava, and a subsequent biopsy identifies small cell lung cancer. Given the high chemosensitivity of this tumor type, what is the most appropriate initial definitive management strategy for his obstructive symptoms?
options: Emergency placement of an endovascular SVC stent
Immediate surgical resection of the mediastinal mass
Administration of systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy alone
correctOption: Administration of systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy alone
optionExplanations: SVC stenting provides rapid relief for most patients but chemotherapy is preferred as first-line for highly sensitive tumors like small cell.
Anticoagulation manages thrombus-related SVCO but does not treat the extrinsic compression caused by the tumor mass.
Surgical resection is rarely the initial treatment for SVCO, especially in small cell lung cancer which is a systemic disease.
Radiotherapy is an option for SVCO but is usually reserved for non-chemosensitive tumors or where chemotherapy is not indicated.
Small cell lung cancer, germ cell tumors, and lymphomas are highly chemosensitive; chemotherapy can resolve the obstruction rapidly.
